questions.stem: A radioactive substance has a half-life of 5 years. What fraction of the original sample remains after 20 years?

options.option_text: 1/16 — 20 years = 4 half-lives; fraction remaining = (1/2)^4 = 1/16
1/4 — this corresponds to only 2 half-lives (10 years), not 20 years
1/8 — this corresponds to 3 half-lives (15 years), not 20 years
1/20 — divides by 20 linearly; radioactive decay is exponential, not linear

questions.explanation: HALF-LIFE: time for half the radioactive atoms to decay. FORMULA: N = N0 x (1/2)^n where n = number of half-lives. n = 20/5 = 4 half-lives. Fraction remaining = (1/2)^4 = 1/16. DECAY TABLE: 1 half-life → 1/2; 2 → 1/4; 3 → 1/8; 4 → 1/16; 5 → 1/32. CARBON-14 DATING: half-life 5,730 years; used to date organic material up to ~50,000 years. URANIUM-238: half-life 4.5 billion years; used for geological dating. PYQ: half-life calculation in SSC CGL, IBPS PO physics — 1-2x per cycle.

questions.stem: In nuclear fission, a heavy nucleus (like U-235) splits into smaller nuclei. This process releases energy because:

options.option_text: The products have greater binding energy per nucleon than the original nucleus, releasing the difference as energy
The total mass of products is greater than the original nucleus, and extra mass converts to energy
Fission creates new protons and neutrons; the energy comes from creating these new particles
Chemical bonds between uranium atoms break releasing stored chemical energy in the nucleus

questions.explanation: BINDING ENERGY: energy needed to disassemble a nucleus into protons and neutrons. BINDING ENERGY PER NUCLEON: peaks at iron-56 (Fe-56). FISSION: heavy nuclei (U-235, Pu-239) have LOWER binding energy per nucleon than mid-sized nuclei (like Kr, Ba). When U-235 splits → products have HIGHER binding energy per nucleon. The DIFFERENCE in binding energy is released (E = mc² — mass defect). FUSION: light nuclei (H-1, H-2) also have lower binding energy per nucleon → fusing them toward iron releases energy. MASS DEFECT: products are LIGHTER than reactants (not heavier) — the lost mass converts to energy. PYQ: why fission releases energy in UPSC GS-3, SSC CGL, IBPS PO.

questions.stem: Alpha particles emitted during radioactive decay consist of:

options.option_text: Two protons and two neutrons (helium-4 nucleus) — identical to a He-4 nucleus with charge +2
High-energy electrons emitted from the nucleus during beta decay — that is a beta particle
High-energy electromagnetic radiation with no charge or mass — that is gamma radiation
A single proton ejected from the nucleus under high nuclear pressure (not this)

questions.explanation: THREE TYPES OF RADIOACTIVE DECAY: ALPHA (α): 2 protons + 2 neutrons = He-4 nucleus. Charge = +2. LEAST penetrating (stopped by paper or skin). Most ionising. BETA (β): electron (β-) or positron (β+) emitted from nucleus. Moderately penetrating (stopped by aluminium sheet). GAMMA (γ): high-energy electromagnetic radiation (photons). Most penetrating (needs thick lead/concrete). No charge, no mass. DECAY EQUATIONS: Alpha decay → atomic number decreases by 2, mass number decreases by 4. Beta- decay → atomic number increases by 1 (neutron → proton + electron + antineutrino). PYQ: alpha/beta/gamma properties in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, UPSC physics.

questions.stem: In a nuclear reactor, control rods made of boron or cadmium are used to:

options.option_text: Absorb excess neutrons and control the rate of the chain reaction
Slow down neutrons to thermal energies (that is the moderator's role, not the control rods)
Reflect neutrons back into the reactor core to increase efficiency
Convert nuclear energy into electrical energy through direct electromagnetic induction

questions.explanation: NUCLEAR REACTOR COMPONENTS: (1) FUEL: enriched U-235 or Pu-239. (2) MODERATOR: heavy water (D2O) or graphite — slows neutrons to thermal energies to sustain chain reaction. (3) CONTROL RODS: boron, cadmium, hafnium — absorb neutrons to CONTROL the reaction rate. Inserted = fewer neutrons available = slower reaction. Withdrawn = more neutrons = faster reaction. (4) COOLANT: water or CO2 — carries heat away. (5) REFLECTOR: reflects neutrons back into core. MODERATOR vs CONTROL RODS: moderator slows neutrons; control rods absorb them. India's RAPS, TAPS use CANDU-type heavy water reactors. PYQ: nuclear reactor components in UPSC GS-3, IBPS PO, SSC CGL.

questions.stem: Nuclear fusion powers the Sun. The primary fusion reaction in the Sun combines:

options.option_text: Hydrogen nuclei (protons) to form helium-4, releasing enormous energy (proton-proton chain)
Uranium atoms to release energy via fission — the Sun uses fusion, not fission
Carbon and oxygen nuclei to form iron at the Sun's core temperature (not this)
Helium nuclei to form hydrogen, which is the reverse of the actual fusion process

questions.explanation: SOLAR FUSION: proton-proton chain reaction. NET REACTION: 4 H-1 → He-4 + 2 positrons + 2 neutrinos + energy. TEMPERATURE NEEDED: ~15 million K (Sun's core temperature). FUSION vs FISSION: fusion = light nuclei combine; fission = heavy nuclei split. BOTH release energy. H-BOMB (thermonuclear bomb): uncontrolled fusion (D-T: deuterium + tritium). ITER/TOKAMAK: experimental controlled fusion reactors (plasma at 150 million K). ADVANTAGE of fusion: fuel is deuterium (from seawater), no long-lived radioactive waste. CHALLENGE: achieving and maintaining the required plasma temperature and pressure. PYQ: solar fusion fuel and reaction in UPSC, SSC CGL, IBPS PO science.

questions.stem: The 'critical mass' of a fissile material is defined as:

options.option_text: The minimum mass required for a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction to occur
The maximum mass of uranium that can be safely stored in a single container
The mass of fuel consumed per unit energy produced in a nuclear reactor
The mass of control rods needed to completely stop a reactor's chain reaction

questions.explanation: CRITICAL MASS: the minimum amount of fissile material (U-235, Pu-239) in which a self-sustaining chain reaction can occur. Below critical mass: too many neutrons escape before causing another fission. At critical mass: exactly one neutron from each fission causes another fission (k = 1; steady state). Above critical mass (supercritical): chain reaction accelerates exponentially → explosion (nuclear bomb). CRITICAL MASS OF U-235: ~52 kg (spherical, no reflector). With a neutron reflector: can be reduced to ~15 kg. IMPLOSION DESIGN: Fat Man (Hiroshima used gun-type; Nagasaki used implosion) — rapidly compresses sub-critical Pu to supercritical. PYQ: critical mass definition in UPSC GS-3, defence current affairs, SSC CGL.

questions.stem: Radioactive iodine-131 (I-131) with a half-life of 8 days is used in thyroid cancer treatment. If a patient receives 160 mg of I-131, how much remains after 32 days?

options.option_text: 20 mg — corresponds to 3 half-lives (24 days); 160 x (1/2)^3 = 20 mg — wrong number of half-lives
40 mg — corresponds to 2 half-lives (16 days); 160 x (1/2)^2 = 40 mg — wrong count
5 mg — corresponds to 5 half-lives (40 days); 160 x (1/2)^5 = 5 mg — wrong time period

questions.explanation: CALCULATION: n = 32/8 = 4 half-lives. Remaining = 160 x (1/2)^4 = 160 x 1/16 = 10 mg. MEDICAL USE: I-131 (radioiodine) concentrates in thyroid tissue → treats hyperthyroidism and differentiated thyroid cancer. EMISSION: beta and gamma rays — kills thyroid cells locally. HALF-LIFE SIGNIFICANCE: 8-day half-life means the dose is mostly gone within 40 days (5 half-lives = ~3% remaining). After 32 days (4 half-lives), only 10/160 = 6.25% remains. PYQ: I-131 half-life calculation in IBPS PO quantitative science or UPSC GS-3 nuclear medicine context.
